title: Clustering
body:
Grouping unlabelled points so that points in a group are close to each other and far from the
other groups. The main task in [[Unsupervised Learning]], and the whole thing rests on one word:
**close**.

## Distance is a modelling choice, not a detail

A data point is a [[Vector]], and closeness is a [[Vector Norm]]. Euclidean distance is the
default:

$$d(x, y) = \sqrt{\sum_i (x_i - y_i)^2}$$

Two consequences that decide whether the result means anything:

- **Scale dominates.** Cluster people by income in dollars and age in years and the income column
  is the only one that matters, because it is numerically thousands of times larger. Standardising
  every feature first is not optional; it changes the answer completely. See [[Mean]] and
  [[Variance]].
- **High dimensions dilute distance.** With enough features every pair of points is roughly
  equidistant and "nearest" stops meaning anything. This is why
  [[Principal Component Analysis]] is usually run first.

Cosine distance ([[Dot Product]]) is the common alternative when direction matters and magnitude
does not, as with text.

## k-means

The algorithm the course means. Pick $k$, then alternate two steps until nothing moves:

```
1. choose k initial centroids
2. ASSIGN: each point joins its nearest centroid
3. UPDATE: each centroid moves to the mean of its members
4. repeat 2 and 3 until assignments stop changing
```

It always converges, because each step can only reduce the total within-cluster distance and there
are finitely many assignments. **It converges to a local optimum, not the best one**, so the
standard practice is several random restarts, keeping the best. k-means++ spreads the initial
centroids apart and mostly fixes it.

### What it assumes, and therefore where it fails

| Assumption | Fails on |
|---|---|
| Clusters are roughly spherical | elongated or curved shapes; two concentric rings are hopeless |
| Similar sizes | one big and one tiny cluster get split wrongly |
| **You know $k$** | the usual case, where you do not |
| Every point belongs somewhere | outliers drag centroids around, since the mean is not robust |

**Choosing $k$ has no correct answer**, which follows from unsupervised learning having no ground
truth. The elbow method plots within-cluster distance against $k$ and looks for the bend;
silhouette scores measure how well each point fits its cluster against the next-best one. Both are
heuristics, and $k = n$ always scores perfectly on the raw distance, which is the reminder that
you are choosing rather than discovering.

Hierarchical clustering (merge the closest pair repeatedly, producing a dendrogram) and DBSCAN
(grow clusters by density, so shapes can be arbitrary and outliers belong to nothing) are the two
answers to those failure rows. Neither is on this course and neither has a note.

## Where it lands in the degree

The centroid is a [[Mean]], the distance is [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]], and the preprocessing is
[[STATISTICS]]. The output is usually the *input* to something else: cluster labels become a
feature for [[Supervised Learning]], or the clusters get named by a person and become segments.
